$comment: Differential conformance corpus. Hand-written INPUT, not generated. tools/generate-conformance-fixtures.ps1 runs every `source` against a real pwsh and records the result under fixtures/; tools/conformance.mts runs every `probe` against this project and compares the two. A case whose probe kind is `none` is an honest admission that the project has nothing to compare yet -- it is counted and reported as unimplemented, never silently passed.

cases.why: The pipeline unrolls ONE level. A recursive flatten reports 3 here; the reference implementation reports 2. This is the case that most often gets implemented wrong.
Counting 2 is not enough: the SECOND item must still be an Object[]. A count of 2 would also be produced by an implementation that turned the inner array into a string.
Unrolling is one level regardless of depth, so a three-deep literal still measures 2.
$null FLOWS through the pipeline: ForEach-Object runs twice for @($null,1). An enumerator that drops nulls stays invisible until a script counts iterations.

Measure-Object reports 1 for the same input ForEach-Object visits twice. That is Measure-Object skipping nulls, NOT the pipeline dropping them -- conflating the two is exactly how the enumerator gets broken.
cases.pending: Measure-Object is declared native-semantic in the manifest but has no implementation yet, so there is nothing to compare. The pipeline half of this pair IS compared, by pipeline.foreach-runs-for-null.

cases.why: An empty array unrolls to zero objects, not to one empty array.
A string is one object, not a sequence of characters. A JS habit -- spreading the string -- gets this wrong.
A hashtable travels as ONE object; it does not unroll into entries. The naive guess is 2.
A non-array value enumerates as itself, exactly once.

By code point 'B' (0x42) is less than 'a' (0x61), so an ordinal implementation answers True. The reference implementation answers False: string comparison is culture-aware. This case caught the original implementation.
The mirror of the above: lowercase 'a' DOES sort before uppercase 'B', which an ordinal comparison denies.
The full ordering, not one pair. Sort-Object is stable, so A/a and b/B keep their input order while grouping by base letter.
Numbers sort numerically. A string-coercing sort puts 10 before 9.
-eq is case-INSENSITIVE. Making the case-sensitive comparison the default disagrees with the reference implementation on the most common operator in the language.
-ceq is the explicit case-sensitive form. Both must exist and must differ.
'10' -lt '9' is True because both sides are strings. A comparator that sniffs numbers out of strings answers False.
PowerShell coerces the RIGHT operand to the LEFT operand's type, so 10 -lt '9' is a NUMERIC comparison and is False. Comparing them as strings answers True.
$null compares less than any string, which is what makes Sort-Object put nulls first.

@(1,2,3) -eq 2 does not return a boolean -- it FILTERS and returns 2. An operator that always returns a boolean is wrong about the whole left-hand-array family. The source asks for the TYPE as well as the value, because a boolean implementation would still print something and could otherwise look close.
[bool]@() is False. JavaScript says [] is truthy, so this is the likeliest place for a JS habit to leak in.
A one-element array takes the truthiness of its element, so @(0) is False.
The other half of the single-element rule.
@(0,0) is True: length greater than 1 wins over the elements. The single-element rule does NOT generalise.
The string "0" is True (non-empty) while the number 0 is False. Coercing the string to a number inverts this.
Pairs with truthy.string-zero; together they pin that the TYPE is consulted, not the text.
An empty string is False; a whitespace string is not.
' ' is True. Trimming before testing emptiness would be wrong.
$null is False.
-1 is True: the rule is 'not zero', not 'positive'.
An EMPTY hashtable is True even though an empty array is False. Treating 'empty container' as one rule breaks one of the two.
A whole-number literal is Int32, not Double. Get-Member reporting Double for 1 would disagree with the reference implementation everywhere.
A fractional literal is Double.
4/2 is Int32, not Double: PowerShell narrows an exact quotient back to an integer type.
1/2 is Double 0.5, not integer 0. C-style integer division would give 0.
A literal past Int32.MaxValue is Int64. A single JS number type cannot see this boundary, so this case exists to make the gap measurable rather than assume it away.
Baseline.
Baseline.
An array literal is Object[], not a typed array, even when every element is an Int32.
Byte[] must stay Byte[]: the native byte channel depends on bytes never being decoded to text.
Get-Date emits a DateTime object, not a formatted string. The value is time-dependent; the TYPE is not.
A property bag reports PSCustomObject as its most-derived type name. Get-Member and the formatter both key on this.
TypeNames is a HIERARCHY, not a label. -is and the formatter both walk it, so the whole chain is part of the contract.
-is accepts the SHORT type name. The formatter's type lookup uses the same rule, so a full-name-only match would silently stop finding format definitions.
$null.GetType() throws InvokeMethodOnNull -- $null is not an object with a type. Reporting System.Object for it is a convenient fiction, and this records it rather than hiding it.
cases.pending: typeNameOf(null) returns 'System.Object' as a total-function convenience, and the reference implementation throws instead, so there is no honest scalar to compare. Recorded in known-differences.yml as typename-of-null-is-total.

cases.why: $o.name and $o.Name are the same property. A Map keyed by the exact string silently misses.

A missing property and a property HOLDING null both read as $null, but they must stay distinguishable or Where-Object { $_.X -eq $null } matches objects that have no X at all. The reference implementation is asked whether the member exists, not what it reads as.
Property order is the order Format-Table renders columns in. Alphabetising it would change every table.
Existence checks follow the same case rule as reads.

-replace is case-INSENSITIVE by default, so 'ABC' -replace 'b','x' is 'AxC'. Every regex engine defaults the other way, so copying a JavaScript RegExp's default would be wrong here and on -match, -like and -split with it.
-like is case-insensitive and uses wildcards, not regex. The wildcard language is genuinely different: '.' and '+' are literals, the escape character is a backtick, and [!a] does NOT negate.

-split returns an array whose Count is observable. The probe answers a count rather than the array because the source asks pwsh for .Count, and comparing a list against that Int32 would fail for the wrong reason.

PowerShell's OWN number-to-string conversion is culture-INVARIANT: "$(1.5)" is '1.5' even under a culture whose decimal separator is a comma. Assuming it follows the culture is a classic error, and the capture's culture passes settle it empirically.
cases.pending: The project has no value-to-string conversion layer yet. Captured now so the invariant is on record before that layer is written.

cases.why: The .NET .ToString() call DOES follow the culture, unlike interpolation. Pairing it with culture.interpolation-is-invariant is what makes the distinction visible instead of theoretical.
-f formatting is culture-dependent in both the group and the decimal separator. Captured under the pinned culture; the culture passes record what a differently-configured host produces.

$? is True after a command that succeeded. Capturing it at all is delicate: invoking through `& $scriptblock` MASKS the inner failure and always reports True, so the capture has to read $? inside the evaluated source.
cases.pending: The kernel that would set $? is not built; streams.ts defines the ErrorRecord it will carry. Captured now so the harness is ready for it.

cases.why: $? is False after a NON-TERMINATING error, even though nothing threw. A harness that reports True here is measuring its own wrapper rather than PowerShell.
$LASTEXITCODE carries a NATIVE process's exit code, which is a different channel from $?. Spawning the running pwsh keeps the case platform-neutral.
cases.passesReason: Spawns a child pwsh. Deterministic by construction -- a literal exit code -- so the repeat and culture passes would only buy three more process launches.
cases.pending: No native process channel in the browser build; NativeStreams is declared but nothing drives it.

cases.why: Scripts branch on FullyQualifiedErrorId, so it is part of the observable contract. This checks the project's composition rule -- `<ErrorId>,<CommandName>` -- against what the reference implementation actually produces.
CategoryInfo.Category is a CLOSED enum that streams.ts reproduces by name. A category invented by hand would not survive this check.
Parameter-validation failures have their own error-id shape, distinct from a command's runtime errors. Binding is where most version-to-version breakage lives, so its error shape matters.
cases.pending: No binder yet. invocation.ts declares the BindingResult a binder will return; nothing produces one.

cases.why: Calling a method on $null is an engine-level error with a stable id, not a command error -- so the id stands alone, with no ',<CommandName>' suffix. That is why the operator layer builds its ErrorRecord directly instead of through errorRecord(), whose composition rule is right for a cmdlet and wrong here.

Arithmetic errors are TERMINATING in PowerShell, a different control-flow shape from a cmdlet's non-terminating error. Only INTEGER and DECIMAL division raise: a double divided by zero is Infinity, which was measured rather than assumed.
A successful command must add NOTHING to $Error. This guards the CAPTURE: a harness that leaked its own errors into the record would make every case look as if it had failed.
cases.pending: No error-stream driver yet; this case exists to check the capture, not the project.

cases.why: -Sum is a switch, not a boolean. -Sum and -Sum:$false differ, and a family of 7.7 fixes is exactly that distinction.
Whether -InputObject binds from the pipeline decides whether `x | Measure-Object` works at all.
-Property is positional at 0, which is what makes `Sort-Object Length` bind without a parameter name.
-Property is Object[], not String[]: it also accepts calculated-property hashtables and script blocks.
-First is Int32, so -First 'abc' must fail at BINDING rather than inside the command body.
Parameter SETS are what a naive capture loses. Which sets -ExpandProperty belongs to is a fact about the command that the binder cannot be correct without.
-FilterScript is positional at 0, which is why `Where-Object { $_ }` binds the block without a name.
-EQ carries an alias. Losing aliases makes a command reject scripts the reference implementation accepts.
-NoEnumerate is the switch that turns OFF the one-level unroll, so its switch-ness is load-bearing for the pipeline cases above.
-InputObject is positional at 0.
Out-Null's only parameter binds from the pipeline; that is the whole command.
-Count is Int32.
-Maximum is Object, not Int32 -- it accepts doubles, and the argument's type decides whether the result is integral. Declaring it Int32 would silently change the output type.
-Format is String.
-AsUTC is a switch.
-Name is positional at 0 in the all-commands set.
-Syntax is a switch.
-Name is positional at 0, which is why `Get-Help Sort-Object` works.
-Full is a switch.
-Count is Int32.
-Id is Int64[], not Int32 -- history ids are longs, and an array.
-Stack is a switch.
-PSDrive is String[].

A GUID differs on every run. This case PROVES the normaliser earns its keep: without the guid rule the two determinism passes disagree and the capture fails. Now that New-Guid exists it also measures the SHAPE it emits: a value that is not canonical 8-4-4-4-12 hex would not match the rule, and the comparison would fail.

The working directory is machine-specific and leaks into output. Canonicalising it to <REPO> is what lets a fixture captured here reproduce anywhere. It is also the one behavioural claim Get-Location makes: PathInfo.Path is the working directory VERBATIM, so any decoration would stop the rule matching.
The wall clock is genuinely unstable. Declaring the case volatile WITH A REASON is the only way past the residue check, which proves the check cannot be bypassed by accident.
cases.volatile: Reads the wall clock, so the value is a bare year that the residue scanner is right to flag. Declared here so the scanner's refusal is exercised by a case that is expected to survive it.

cases.why: A ONE-CHARACTER -Format is a STANDARD specifier, never a custom one: 'M' is the month-and-day pattern, not the month number. Reading it as custom is the single most likely way to get -Format wrong, and it is silent.
The mirror of the case above: TWO characters make the same letter a custom specifier, so 'MM' is the zero-padded month. The rule is about length, not about the letter.

'H' is a valid CUSTOM specifier but not a standard one, so a lone 'H' is REJECTED rather than treated as the hour. An implementation that silently formatted it would disagree with the reference implementation by producing an answer where there is none.
Three letters give the abbreviation and four the full name, for both days and months. The names are en-US invariant here because the capture pins the culture.
'hh' is the 12-hour clock and 'HH' the 24-hour one; at 05:06 they agree, which is why 'tt' is in the same string — it is what makes the pair readable at all.
A .NET DateTime keeps 100-nanosecond ticks, so 'fffffff' has seven digits and the shorter forms TRUNCATE rather than round. A millisecond-only model cannot produce 0089000.

Ticks is 6.39e17, past Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER. A JavaScript number would silently lose the low digits, so the value has to be a bigint. Compared as text precisely so the comparison itself cannot round it.
Format-List follows declaration order, so the order is part of the contract and not a detail. Get-Date ADDS DisplayHint as a NoteProperty; a bare [datetime] has no such member.
%u and %w are different numbering schemes that happen to AGREE on a Wednesday. Recorded so its Sunday twin below is visibly the discriminating case rather than an arbitrary second example.
The discriminating case: on a Sunday %u is 7 (ISO, Monday-first) and %w is 0 (C, Sunday-first). An implementation that used one number for both passes the Wednesday case and fails here.
Three week numberings that disagree on the same day: %V is ISO-8601, %U counts from the first Sunday and %W from the first Monday. Only %V is 10.

The padding is the whole difference between these pairs: %d is zero-padded and %e SPACE-padded, %H zero-padded and %k space-padded. Trimming either would look like a cosmetic tidy-up and change the output width.
An unrecognised specifier drops the percent and KEEPS the letter rather than erroring or passing the pair through. Guessed either way, this is wrong.
%% is a literal percent. Needed because the previous case makes an unknown specifier swallow its percent, so the escape has to be distinguishable from it.
THE case for the bound. Two hundred draws from [0,1) produce only 0, which is possible only if -Maximum is exclusive. An inclusive implementation yields 0 and 1 and fails here.
The other half: [0,2) really does produce both 0 and 1, so the case above is about exclusivity and not about the generator being stuck.
Minimum equal to Maximum is a TERMINATING argument error, not a degenerate range that always returns the bound. The obvious implementation answers 5; the reference implementation refuses.
The id alone is not the whole contract: the message names both values, and a script or a user reads it. Compared verbatim so a reworded message is a visible change.
-Count 5 over three items returns THREE, each exactly once: it is a sample without replacement, capped at the list length, not five draws with repeats.
HistoryInfo is an OBJECT, not a numbered line, and Duration is DERIVED from the two timestamps rather than stored beside them. The order is what Format-List follows.

A command with no MAML help file gets AUTO-GENERATED help, and its chain is ExtendedCmdletHelpInfo, not MamlCommandHelpInfo. Every command in this project is in that position, so picking the MAML shape — which the first implementation did — was wrong.

-Full changes the TYPE NAME and nothing else, and it adds a #FullView twin for EVERY base name — six entries, not two. That is the whole Get-Help finding: the view is a formatting decision, so the object is unchanged.
-Parameter is the one switch that really does return a different object. Its members differ from the MAML descriptor's, which is the second half of the shape mix-up above.
Get-Command emits typed CommandInfo objects, and the formatter keys off the chain. A single label would be indistinguishable from the alias case below.
An alias reports AliasInfo even though the command behind it is a cmdlet, and reports its OWN name. Resolving the alias to its target would answer a different question.

The key ORDER is what the Name/Value table renders, and PSVersion is first rather than alphabetical. Nine keys, and none of them invented: OS and Platform describe the simulated machine, and the version comes from the resolved profile.
